name: Nāgārjuna

tradition.text: born four hundred years after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa (Laṅkāvatāra prophecy); Tibetan histories give him a life of six hundred years

places: Nālandā (ordination and abbacy in Tibetan accounts)

realization_account.text: The Laṅkāvatāra prophesies that a monk named Nāga will destroy the views of existence and non-existence, teach the supreme Mahāyāna and reach the Joyful ground (pramuditā bhūmi) before going to Sukhāvatī. The Chinese Life tells that as a brahmin youth he misused an art of invisibility, narrowly escaped death, renounced, exhausted the available scriptures and received the Mahāyāna sūtras from a great nāga in the nāga palace. Tibetan histories (Bu-ston, Tāranātha) tell that he was ordained at Nālandā, became its abbot, brought the Perfection of Wisdom in 100,000 lines back from the nāgas, practised alchemy, advised a Sātavāhana king and at the end gave his head to a prince who severed it with a blade of kuśa grass.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Scholarly account: a South Indian monk of c. 150–250 CE connected with the Sātavāhana court; the name was borne also by later authors (a tantric Nāgārjuna and the alchemist tch:nagarjuna-siddha), which the tradition conflates. The 'reasoning corpus' (MMK, VV, ŚS, YṢ, VP) and the RĀ and SL are widely accepted; other attributions are disputed. Laṅkāvatāra prophecy verse number (c. 10.165–166) to check.
summary: Founder of the Madhyamaka: author of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and the other 'reasoning' treatises, of letters to a Sātavāhana king and of hymns, revered in every Mahāyāna tradition as the 'second Buddha' who opened the Perfection of Wisdom teaching of emptiness.

name: Āryadeva

realization_account.text: The Chinese Life tells that he offered his own eye to a great statue of Maheśvara, defeated the teachers of other schools in debate, and was killed by a disciple of a defeated opponent, whom he forgave while dying, teaching that there is no one who kills and no one who is killed. Tibetan accounts make him the adopted son of a Sinhalese king, born from a lotus, who defeated the Śaiva debater Mātṛceṭa at Nālandā and converted him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The tantric works under this name (e.g. Caryāmelāpakapradīpa) are by a later Āryadeva (scholarly account).
summary: Nāgārjuna's principal disciple, author of the Four Hundred Verses (Catuḥśataka), which joins the bodhisattva's practice to the refutation of permanent entities, the self and extreme views.

name: Rāhulabhadra

realization_account.text: In some Tibetan accounts the brahmin Rāhulabhadra (identified with Saraha) ordained Nāgārjuna at Nālandā; in the Chinese lineage of the Dharma-treasure he follows Kāṇadeva (Āryadeva).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Conflicting placements are both the traditions' accounts; not reconciled here.
summary: Early Madhyamaka poet to whom the Hymn to the Perfection of Wisdom is ascribed; the lineage accounts place him either as Nāgārjuna's teacher (Tibetan) or as a successor of Āryadeva (Chinese patriarch lists).

name: Buddhapālita

realization_account.text: Tāranātha relates that he studied Nāgārjuna's works under Saṃgharakṣita, attained realization through the practice of Mañjuśrī, and taught at Dantapurī.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Tāranātha details from memory, low confidence.
summary: Commentator on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā whose method of drawing out the opponent's unwanted consequences was criticized by Bhāviveka and defended by Candrakīrti, and who is therefore counted as the first 'Prāsaṅgika'.

name: Bhāviveka

realization_account.text: Xuanzang records that Bhāviveka, wishing to debate the Yogācāra master Dharmapāla and failing to meet him, resolved to wait for Maitreya to settle his doubts, recited a dhāraṇī before an image of Avalokiteśvara and entered a rock palace of the asuras to await Maitreya's coming.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Xuanzang's story from memory (moderate); the later works under the name Bhavya are assigned by scholars to other authors.
summary: Madhyamaka master who introduced Dignāga's formal inference into Madhyamaka, criticized Buddhapālita, and in the Madhyamakahṛdaya and Tarkajvālā surveyed and answered the Śrāvaka, Yogācāra, Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Vedānta and Mīmāṃsā schools; regarded in Tibet as the founder of Svātantrika.

name: Avalokitavrata
summary: Author of the vast sub-commentary on Bhāviveka's Prajñāpradīpa, a principal source on the history of the early Madhyamaka commentators and their opponents.

name: Candrakīrti

realization_account.text: Tibetan histories tell that he studied under Kamalabuddhi, a disciple of Buddhapālita, became abbot of Nālandā and debated the lay master Candragomin there for years; to show that things lack own-nature he milked a painted cow and distributed the milk to the monks.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Scholarly account: 7th c.; the tantric commentator of the same name (Pradīpoddyotana) is regarded by scholars as a later author.
summary: Author of the Prasannapadā and the Madhyamakāvatāra, who defended Buddhapālita's method against Bhāviveka, rejected autonomous inference and own-nature at every level, and became for Tibetan traditions the definitive interpreter of Nāgārjuna (the Prāsaṅgika).

name: Kamalabuddhi
summary: In Tibetan accounts a disciple of Buddhapālita and teacher of Candrakīrti.

name: Śāntideva

realization_account.text: A prince who, on the eve of his coronation, saw Mañjuśrī seated on the throne in a dream and renounced; at Nālandā he seemed only to eat, sleep and relieve himself ('Bhusuku'); asked to recite before the assembly, he taught the Bodhicaryāvatāra and at the verse 'when neither being nor non-being remains before the mind' (9.34) rose into the sky and vanished, while his voice continued; the Śikṣāsamuccaya was later found in his cell (Bu-ston; Tāranātha; a Nepalese Sanskrit hagiography).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Hagiographical details from memory (moderate). Scholarly: an earlier shorter recension of the BCA survives in Dunhuang.
summary: Nālandā monk-poet, author of the Bodhicaryāvatāra and the Śikṣāsamuccaya, the classic Indian manuals of the bodhisattva's awakening mind, patience, exchange of self and other and wisdom.

name: Prajñākaramati
notes: Tibetan accounts name him one of the gate-keeper scholars (dvārapaṇḍita) of Vikramaśīla — to check.
summary: Vikramaśīla scholar, author of the chief Sanskrit commentary on the Bodhicaryāvatāra.

name: Jñānagarbha
summary: Author of the Satyadvayavibhaṅga on the two truths; student of Śrīgupta and teacher of Śāntarakṣita in the Tibetan lineage.

name: Śrīgupta
summary: Madhyamaka author of the Tattvāvatāravṛtti; in the Tibetan lineage the teacher of Jñānagarbha.

name: Śāntarakṣita
alt_names: Khenpo Bodhisattva (mkhan po bo dhi sa twa)

tradition.text: invited to Tibet by King Trisong Detsen; with Padmasambhava founded Samye

realization_account.text: Invited to Tibet, he taught the ten virtues and dependent origination; when local spirits obstructed the work he advised the king to invite Padmasambhava; he consecrated Samye, ordained the first seven Tibetan monks and, foreseeing a dispute over the view, left instructions that his student Kamalaśīla be invited to answer it.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Abbot of Nālandā who synthesized Madhyamaka, Yogācāra and Dharmakīrti's epistemology (Madhyamakālaṃkāra, Tattvasaṅgraha), founded Samye and ordained the first Tibetan monks.

name: Kamalaśīla

tradition.text: debated at Samye in the reign of Trisong Detsen

realization_account.text: Tibetan histories (the sBa bzhed and later) tell that he was invited on Śāntarakṣita's instruction, debated Moheyan before the king at Samye, was declared victor so that the gradual path of the six perfections became the norm in Tibet, wrote the Bhāvanākramas at the king's request, and was later murdered.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Samye debate date c. 792–794 in scholarly reconstructions; the Chinese Dunhuang sources give Moheyan's side as victorious.
summary: Śāntarakṣita's disciple, author of the Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, the Madhyamakāloka and the three Bhāvanākramas, who defended the gradual path at the Samye debate against the Chan master Moheyan.

name: Haribhadra (Buddhist)

realization_account.text: Tāranātha makes him a student of Śāntarakṣita and of Vairocanabhadra, who composed his commentaries after a vision of Maitreya, under the patronage of the Pāla king Dharmapāla.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Commentator on the Abhisamayālaṃkāra and the Perfection of Wisdom (Āloka, Sphuṭārthā) in the Yogācāra-Madhyamaka line; not the Jain Haribhadra Sūri (tch:haribhadra).

name: Ārya Vimuktisena
summary: Early commentator on the Abhisamayālaṃkāra; classed by Tibetan doxographers among the Yogācāra-Svātantrika.

name: Jayānanda (Madhyamaka)

realization_account.text: Tibetan accounts record a debate between Jayānanda and the Tibetan logician Chapa Chökyi Senge on Candrakīrti's rejection of autonomous reasoning; the accounts differ on its outcome.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Kashmiri Madhyamaka scholar of the 12th century, author of the only Indian sub-commentary on the Madhyamakāvatāra, active in Tibet and among the Tanguts; distinct from the Bengali Vaiṣṇava poet Jayānanda (tch:jayananda).

name: Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna
summary: U40 contribution: Vikramaśīla master who held Candrakīrti's Madhyamaka to be the correct view and taught it in Tibet in the Satyadvayāvatāra and Madhyamakopadeśa.

name: Bodhibhadra
summary: Nālandā master, commentator on the Jñānasārasamuccaya, and one of Atiśa's teachers.

name: Jitāri
summary: Buddhist logician and doxographer (Sugatamatavibhaṅga), classed by Tibetan doxographers among the false-aspectarian Yogācāra-Madhyamaka; one of Atiśa's teachers.

name: Ratnākaraśānti
summary: U40 contribution: Vikramaśīla master whose Prajñāpāramitopadeśa and Madhyamakālaṃkāropadeśa combine a Yogācāra account of luminous mind with Madhyamaka; classed by some as a Yogācāra-Madhyamaka.

name: Abhayākaragupta
summary: Late Vikramaśīla master (c. 1100), author of the Munimatālaṃkāra, a summa of Madhyamaka doctrine, as well as tantric works.

name: Maitrīpa
summary: U40 contribution: author of the Tattvaratnāvalī, whose doxography divides Madhyamaka into the illusion-like non-dualists and the proponents of the non-foundation of all dharmas, the latter being his own view.

name: Piṅgala (Qingmu 青目)
notes: The Sanskrit form Piṅgala is a reconstruction of Qingmu ('blue eyes').
summary: Author of the commentary on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā translated by Kumārajīva as the Zhong lun; nothing further is known of him.

name: Kumārajīva
summary: U40 contribution: Kuchean translator (d. c. 409/413 CE) whose Chinese versions of the Madhyamaka treatises (Zhong lun, Shiermen lun, Bai lun, Da zhidu lun) founded East Asian Madhyamaka.

name: Devaśarman
notes: Known only from later lists (from memory).
summary: Early commentator on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā whose commentary is lost; known from Avalokitavrata's list of commentators.

name: Guṇamati (commentator on the MMK)
notes: Identity with the Yogācāra Guṇamati uncertain.
summary: Commentator on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā named in Avalokitavrata's list; his commentary is lost. Possibly the Yogācāra master of that name.

name: Vasu (commentator on the Śataśāstra)
summary: Author of the commentary on Āryadeva's verses in the Bai lun translated by Kumārajīva; otherwise unknown.

name: Ajitamitra
notes: The commentary is D4159 (catalog:Derge-Tengyur:D4159); author's name from memory.
summary: Author of the Indian commentary on Nāgārjuna's Ratnāvalī preserved in Tibetan (Ratnāvalīṭīkā).

name: Parahita
notes: Attribution of D3868 to Parahita from memory; to check.
summary: Kashmiri scholar credited with a commentary on the Śūnyatāsaptati (D3868) and with work on Madhyamaka texts in the 11th century.
